question: Did California's AB 1228 minimum wage for workers at large limited-service restaurant chains ($20 per hour from 1 April 2024; signed 28 September 2023) change employment in California's limited-service restaurants (NAICS 722513) over its first eight quarters, 2024Q2-2026Q1, relative to limited-service restaurants in other states, and did the effect change between the first and the second year, when the policy's bite fell? The published QCEW-based studies disagree (Clemens, Edwards, Meer and Nguyen, NBER w34033 revised 2026: a decline of about 3.5%; Dube, NBER w35171, 2026: near zero). This is a pre-specified update of a contested question, not a new question: the latest published QCEW window ends in 2025Q4 (Clemens et al., w35931), so the data add one preliminary quarter, 2026Q1; the 2026Q2 release is due on 2 December 2026 and the crew does not wait for it.
hypotheses: H1 (first stage, in weekly earnings): the pooled 2024Q2-2026Q1 ATT on log average weekly wage (QCEW weekly earnings per job, not the hourly wage the law sets; fewer hours would bias it toward zero) of California NAICS 722513 relative to the comparison group, with the primary estimator fixed at the design gate, is positive: one-sided test at 5%. The inference method must be valid with a single treated state (Ferman-Pinto, conformal, or a permutation whose comparison pool is large enough that a 5% test is attainable without California ranking first by construction); standard errors clustered by state are not used. The run level-mde, after the design gate and before any run that reads post-2023Q3 outcomes, on data through 2019Q4 only, reports the level evidence the design specifies (rejection rates of the procedure on placebo units, by size); for California itself the level is argued from the conservative standard error and critical value, not measured, and the paper says so. Reported also for each year separately, because the $20 fast-food wage did not rise in 2025 or 2026 while California's general minimum did (its premium fell from $4.00 to $3.10). If H1 fails, H2 is reported as uninformative about the wage floor.

H2 (main): the pooled 2024Q2-2026Q1 ATT on log employment of California NAICS 722513, same estimator and inference. Decision rule, fixed now, with b = 0.02 log points: compute the two-sided 95% CI [L, U] and the 90% CI [l, u] (a two one-sided test at 5%) with the H1 inference method. Sign: 'negative' if U < 0, 'positive' if L > 0, else 'sign undetermined'. Size: 'smaller than b' if -b < l and u < b, 'at least b' if u < -b or l > b, else 'size undetermined'. The headline label is the pair, in this exhaustive and mutually exclusive table: (negative, at least b) = 'decline of at least 2%'; (negative, smaller than b) = 'decline smaller than 2%'; (negative, size undetermined) = 'decline, size not distinguishable from 2%'; (sign undetermined, smaller than b) = 'no effect as large as 2%'; (sign undetermined, at least b) = 'inconclusive'; (sign undetermined, size undetermined) = 'inconclusive'; and the positive cases symmetrically ('increase of at least 2%', 'increase smaller than 2%', 'increase, size not distinguishable from 2%'). The bound: the published pooled weekly-wage effects are about 6% (Clemens et al., two-year, 2026 revision) to 7% (Dube 2026, Table 1 Panel A, SDID), close but not identical estimands; at those wage effects -0.02 is an own-wage elasticity of about -0.29 to -0.33. Clemens et al.'s revised two-year QCEW estimates range from -2.02% to -5.03%, so the least negative of them sits at the bound: a CI inside +/-0.02 excludes their median and detrended estimates, not every one of their specifications, and a CI wholly below -0.02 excludes Dube's SDID estimate. The run level-mde (after the design gate, before any run that reads post-2023Q3 outcomes, on data through 2019Q4 only) computes the minimum detectable effect at 80% power and the other power quantities the design lists, and the paper reports them next to H2. Timing for H1-H3, fixed now: the base period is 2023Q3, the last quarter before AB 1228 was signed (2022Q3-2023Q3 is not policy-free: AB 257, enacted September 2022 and stayed in January 2023, would have allowed a fast-food wage of up to $22; the design reports a pre-AB 257 base as a robustness check); 2023Q4 and 2024Q1 (between signing and the effective date) enter neither the base nor the pooled post-period and are reported separately as a report-only anticipation estimate, as Sosinskiy and Reich (2026, Table A3) already report them; Dube (2026, Table 1 Panel B), whose base is the 2022Q1-2023Q3 mean so that 2023Q4 stays out of it, is the published result closest to this timing and is named as such in the paper; Dube's 2023Q4 base is a pre-specified robustness check, not an alternative primary. Choice of the primary specification, fixed now because the published literature already maps each choice to its result (w35931; Dube 2026, Table D1) and the PI has read that map: the design gate does not pick the estimator, detrending, outcome normalization, comparison pool or fitting window by judgement. The Designer lists a candidate set covering both published approaches (at least: DD and DD with a state-specific linear trend fitted on the pre-period, each on log employment and on log employment per capita; synthetic control; SDID; with the comparison pools both studies use), and the primary is the candidate with the smallest root mean squared error of placebo-in-time pooled ATTs at pseudo-treatment dates that use only data before 2023Q3 (the pseudo-dates, their windows and the tie-break are fixed in the design). Two named secondary analyses are reported whatever the rule picks: Clemens et al.'s detrended indexed DD and Dube's SDID, both re-estimated with the 2023Q3 timing above. The study is therefore pre-specified but not blind, and the paper says so.

H3 (reduced-form year two minus year one): the ATT on log employment for 2025Q2-2026Q1 minus that for 2024Q2-2025Q1, same estimator and inference, reported next to the yearly H1 wage effects (and the implied yearly own-wage elasticities), because the policy's bite fell in year two and a change cannot be attributed to time alone. 'Larger decline in year two' if the 95% CI of the difference is below 0, 'smaller decline in year two' if above 0, otherwise 'no detectable change'. If the pre-period MDE of the difference exceeds 0.04 (twice b), H3 is reported as uninformative whatever the estimate.
contribution: A pre-specified (not blind) update with modest novelty, stated as such: the estimand, base period, a rule that picks the primary estimator from pre-2023Q3 data only, inference valid with a single treated state and decision rules are fixed and reviewed before any post-2023Q3 outcome is computed; H2 adds an equivalence test against a 2% bound meant to separate the two published readings (level-mde, run before any post-period outcome, showed that at this design's precision the test cannot reach 'smaller than 2%': h90 0.054 > b, so it cannot separate them; the paper says so); H3 compares year two with year one next to the yearly wage effects, because the fast-food premium over California's general minimum fell from $4.00 to $3.10; the data add one preliminary quarter (2026Q1) to the latest published window (2025Q4). Decompositions of the published disagreement (Dube 2026, Tables D1-D2; Clemens et al. w35931, Table A1; Sosinskiy and Reich 2026, Appendix A) and published anticipation and base-period checks (Dube 2026, Table 1 Panel B; Sosinskiy and Reich 2026, Table A3; w35931, footnote 5) are cited, not repeated as findings. The PI and the Scout know the published estimates and a published descriptive California-vs-rest-of-US index for 722513 through March 2026 and a weekly-wage index on the same page (Recording Law data page, 6 November 2026; the PI read its March 2026 employment values, California 97.06 against 98.99, and its 2026Q1 weekly-wage values, 114.8 against 104.3, in the Scout's and the Reviewer's reports) (disclosed); the analysing roles compute nothing on post-period outcomes before the design gate. Limits known now: QCEW counts jobs and weekly earnings, not hours or hourly wages; part of NAICS 722513 is outside the law's coverage (Melo et al. 2026 put covered-chain employment about one-third below QCEW 722513 in California in 2025, so roughly two-thirds is covered), so effects on covered jobs are diluted; Melo et al. also argue that QCEW 722513 tracks covered-chain employment poorly over time and across comparison states (gaps in 2019-2025 changes of -8 to +17 points, far larger than the 2% bound), a measurement limit this design cannot remove; covered chains are also coded in NAICS 722515 and 722511 (Melo et al.), so neither is a clean control; county cells are suppressed more often from 2025, so the design must say whether the analysis is at state or county level; 2026Q1 is preliminary and will be revised.

design.summary: State-level comparison of California's private NAICS 722513 employment (quarterly mean of the three monthly QCEW levels, seasonally adjusted with fixed 2014-2019 state factors) with donor states over 2024Q2-2026Q1 relative to the base quarter 2023Q3. 2023Q4-2024Q1 is held out as a report-only anticipation window, and 2020Q1-2021Q4 is excluded from every fitting window. The primary estimator and pool are not chosen by judgement. One logged analysis run reads only a panel truncated at 2019Q4. It picks the candidate with the smallest root mean squared error of California's placebo pooled ATTs on log employment at six pre-COVID pseudo-treatment dates (2016Q1-2017Q2). The 24 candidates are: DD and pre-trend-adjusted DD, each with CEM-style aggregate or Dube-style population weights; demeaned synthetic control; and synthetic DID. Each is fitted on log employment or log employment per capita, with Dube's 20 federal-minimum states or with all 50 other states and DC. Inference is a placebo t-test whose SE is the larger of the population-scaled (Ferman-Pinto as implemented by Dube) and the unscaled placebo SE, which is conservative for California, the largest unit, whatever the mix of size-related and state-level noise. Its critical values are the more conservative of t at nu = min(J, the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom of that SE, estimated from each donor's pre-COVID placebo variance) and the quantiles of placebo tests on the ten most populous federal-minimum (D20) states at pre-COVID pseudo-dates; this is computed in level-mde, after the design gate and before any post-2023Q3 outcome is read, on data ending 2019Q4. For SDID statistics the critical values also have a Monte Carlo floor, because SDID's placebo t over-rejected at t_J in check-methods (design.method C1). H1 (log weekly wage), H2 (sign x size rule, b = 0.02) and H3 (year two minus year one) then use the selected estimator and pool. Both camps' specifications (CEM detrended indexed DD, Dube SDID) are named secondaries; their labels are reported next to the primary's in the abstract, and the headline is stated as not robust to either if its sign category differs. Pre-specified robustness and placebo checks (Dube's 2023Q4 base, a pre-AB 257 2022Q2 base, the other pool, NAICS 7225, the final-data window, non-722513 employment, NAICS 722511) are reported whatever they show.
design.estimand: tau = (1/8) * sum over t in 2024Q2..2026Q1 of [Y_CA,t(1) - Y_CA,t(0)] - [Y_CA,2023Q3(1) - Y_CA,2023Q3(0)], where Y is seasonally adjusted log employment (quarterly mean of the three monthly levels) of private NAICS 722513 establishments in California and Y(0) is the path without AB 1228. If AB 1228 had no effect before its signing (28 September 2023, after the September pay period), the second bracket is zero. tau is an intent-to-treat effect on the whole industry code, covered and uncovered establishments together, and in log points (reported also as 100*(exp(tau)-1) percent and as jobs). H1: the same with log average weekly wage. H3: tau_2 - tau_1, with year 1 = 2024Q2-2025Q1 and year 2 = 2025Q2-2026Q1. Candidates on log(employment/population) estimate the same tau, under the maintained assumption that AB 1228 did not change California's resident population; this is why the selection rule can compare all candidates on one scale (F16).
design.identifying_assumption: Without AB 1228, California's seasonally adjusted log 722513 employment (H1: log weekly wage) after 2023Q3 would have stayed as far from the selected counterfactual as it was before. For DD candidates the reference is the 2023Q3 gap, with the pre-period gap trend extrapolated for the trend variant. For synthetic control the reference is the pre-period mean gap; for SDID it is the time-weighted pre-period gap. The rule's premise is that the candidate that reproduced California's actual path best at pre-COVID pseudo-dates is the one for which this holds best. That path includes California's own general minimum-wage phase-in (July 2014 to $15 in 2022; Wiltshire et al., notes section 10), which is part of Y(0) for AB 1228; so the premise is fit to California's path under its own general-MW ramp, and it assumes that whatever lets a candidate track that ramp in 2016-2019 (a gap trend, or R50 donors with their own increases) still tracks California's AB 1228-free path in 2024-2026, when the general minimum rose more slowly (T17). The data would contradict the assumption if: (i) the selected candidate's placebo RMSE is near or above b = 0.02 (reported by select); (ii) the event path shows systematic gaps over 2022Q1-2023Q3 (event-path). That is an out-of-fit test only for DD. For DDT those seven quarters are the trend's fit points, so the gaps there test curvature only, and DDT's out-of-fit pre-period evidence is the 2014-2019 segment of the path; for SC and SDID all non-COVID pre-period quarters are in the fit window F, so the path shows in-sample fit. For DDT, SC and SDID the out-of-fit pre-period evidence is select's placebo RMSE (design-r2 D11); (iii) employment outside 722513 shows an effect (plc-nonff); or (iv) the estimate moves materially with the base (rob-base-2023q4, rob-pre-ab257) or with the pool (rob-pool). None of these checks can confirm the assumption.
design.method: SOFTWARE: Python 3.14.6, numpy 2.5.3, scipy 1.18.1, pandas 3.0.5, statsmodels 0.15.0. Code/requirements.txt is frozen from a fresh venv (matplotlib, imported only by the figure scripts, is pinned in it too; IMPLEMENTATION CHOICES 14); StatsPAI 1.43.0 may be used only as a cross-check in check-methods, never in a run that produces a claim. Nothing in a study run is random (the check-methods Monte Carlo uses numpy default_rng(20261121); its SDID calibration draws use a separate default_rng(20261122), CHECK-METHODS CONSEQUENCES C1). Weights are solved by scipy.optimize.minimize (SLSQP, simplex constraints, start at uniform weights, ftol 1e-12, maxiter 2000); the tests check the KKT conditions to 1e-6. NOTATION: B is the base quarter: 2023Q3 for the real analysis, B' for a pseudo-date. COVID quarters C = 2020Q1-2021Q4 (Dube's exclusion) are never used in any fit, base, trend or SE calculation, with one stated exception: S1 (sec-cemn), which keeps CEM's endpoint trend (g_B - g_{B-8})/8 and so uses g_2021Q3 for the real B, as CEM do (deviation D2; design-r2 D10). At pseudo-dates B'-8 is never a COVID quarter. Fit window F(B) = all quarters from 2014Q1 to B that are not in C. Anticipation window A(B) = {B+1, B+2}. Post window P(B) = B+3..B+10 (8 quarters); year 1 = B+3..B+6; year 2 = B+7..B+10. For the real B these are F = 2014Q1-2019Q4 plus 2022Q1-2023Q3 (31 quarters), A = 2023Q4-2024Q1 and P = 2024Q2-2026Q1. Time t is the calendar quarter index, so the COVID gap counts as elapsed time in trends. OUTCOMES (per state and per donor aggregate; seasonal adjustment is applied to every series that enters an estimator, after aggregation): E = ln(mean of month1-3 employment); P = SA ln(employment) - ln(population); W = ln(avg_wkly_wage) as BLS publishes it (aggregates: ln(sum of total_qtrly_wages / (13 * sum of mean employment))). SEASONAL ADJUSTMENT, fixed and the same for every run: 2x4 centred moving average m_t = (0.5y_{t-2} + y_{t-1} + y_t + y_{t+1} + 0.5y_{t+2})/4 for t = 2014Q3..2019Q2 (it uses only 2014Q1-2019Q4). The factor s_q is the mean of y_t - m_t over the five quarters of type q, minus the mean of the four s_q. The adjusted series is y_t - s_q(t) for all t. ESTIMATORS (closed forms; g_t = Y_CA,t - Ybar_donor,t): DD: tau = mean_{t in P} g_t - g_B. DDT (CEM-style detrended DD): tau = mean_{t in P} [g_t - g_B - b(t - B)], where b is the OLS slope of g_t on t over the calendar quarters B-8..B that are not in C. For the real B that is 2022Q1-2023Q3 (7 points); for pseudo-dates, 9 points. Equivalent to state-specific linear trends in the weighted 2x2 comparison. Donor average for DD and DDT, two weightings: AGG (CEM): the donor aggregate series, i.e. summed employment, summed population and summed wages, logged. POPW (Dube): population-weighted mean of donor log series, weights pop_j at B. SC (demeaned synthetic control, Doudchenko-Imbens / Ferman-Pinto): simplex weights w minimising sum over F of [(Y_CA,t - Ybar_CA,F) - sum_j w_j (Y_j,t - Ybar_j,F)]^2; tau = mean over P of the same demeaned gap. The demeaned form is needed because California's log employment level lies outside the donors' convex hull. SDID (Arkhangelsky et al. 2021, Algorithm 1, no sparsification): the unit weights (omega0, omega in the simplex) minimise sum over F of (omega0 + sum_j omega_j Y_jt - Y_CA,t)^2 + zeta^2 |F| ||omega||^2. Here zeta = (1 * 8)^(1/4) * sigma_hat, and sigma_hat is computed as Arkhangelsky et al. (2021) eq. (2.2): sigma_hat^2 = sum over donors j and over the pairs of consecutive calendar quarters (t, t+1) both in F of (Delta_jt - Delta_bar)^2, divided by J times the number of such pairs, where Delta_jt = Y_j,t+1 - Y_j,t and Delta_bar is their mean over the same donors and pairs (with no gap this is N_co (T_pre - 1)). The time weights (lambda0, lambda in the simplex) minimise sum_j (lambda0 + sum_{s in F} lambda_s Y_js - mean_{t in window} Y_jt)^2 + (1e-6 sigma_hat)^2 J ||lambda||^2 (the paper's zeta^2 N_co ||lambda||^2 with zeta = 1e-6 sigma_hat, fn 3; N_co = J donors). tau = (mean_window Y_CA - sum_s lambda_s Y_CA,s) - sum_j omega_j (mean_window Y_j - sum_s lambda_s Y_js). omega and zeta are fitted once with the 8-quarter post window and reused for the year windows and the anticipation window; lambda is refitted for each window. For W (H1), each estimator is re-applied to the wage series with the same pool: weights refitted on wages for SC/SDID, the gap trend fitted on wages for DDT, and the same weighting for DD/DDT (F16: H1 uses the selected estimator and pool with log weekly wage as outcome). Dube's reuse of employment weights appears in S2 and in the denominator of the own-wage elasticities (DECISIONS; design-r1 D5). CANDIDATE SET (24, in this order, which is also the last tie-break): for e in [DD, DDT], w in [AGG, POPW], n in [E, P], pool in [D20, R50]: 16 candidates. Then SC x [E, P] x [D20, R50] and SDID x [E, P] x [D20, R50]: 8. Ids look like 'DDT-POPW-P-D20'. SELECTION RULE (run select; input data/derived/state_panel_pre.csv, 2014Q1-2019Q4 only; the single cutoff for the selection, the level check and the MDE is 2019Q4. That is earlier than both 'before 2023Q3' (H2 rule) and 'pre-2023Q4' (H2 MDE), and earlier than AB 257's enactment in September 2022 (literature-r1 L1)): pseudo-dates B' in {2016Q1, 2016Q2, 2016Q3, 2016Q4, 2017Q1, 2017Q2}, California treated, the candidate's pool as donors, windows F(B'), A(B'), P(B') as above, so every pseudo-window ends by 2019Q4 and contains no COVID quarter. B' starts at 2016Q1 because DDT needs B'-8 >= 2014Q1, and stops at 2017Q2 because B'+10 <= 2019Q4. The pseudo-ATT is tau_c(B') in log points; for P candidates it is read on the log-employment scale (F16). It is a fit error relative to California's AB 1228-free path, not an estimate of a zero policy effect: California's 2016-2019 path contains its general minimum-wage ramp, which the donors (D20 entirely, R50 partly) lack, so the rule favours candidates that track that ramp (design-r1 D3; T17). RMSE_c = sqrt(mean over the six B' of tau_c(B')^2). Primary = argmin RMSE_c. Tie-break: RMSEs equal after rounding to 4 decimals, then smaller max |tau_c(B')|, then the earlier candidate in the order above. The rule's parameters were fixed by the Designer on 2026-11-21 without computing any placebo or any statistic of the outcomes; no alternative set of pseudo-dates is computed by anyone (F15a). INFERENCE (H1-H3, anticip, S1, S2, robustness and placebo runs; valid with one treated state; no clustered SEs; design-r1 D1): for a statistic tau_u of treated unit u (u = California in every post-period run), compute the placebo estimate tau_j for each donor j in u's donor set (J donors), treating j as treated with the other J-1 donors (u excluded) and the same estimator, windows and outcome. Two SEs. Scaled: SE_s = sqrt((1/J) sum_j tau_j^2 pop_j(B)/pop_u(B)) (Dube's Ferman-Pinto scaling). Unscaled: SE_n = sqrt((1/J) sum_j tau_j^2). SE = max(SE_s, SE_n). Reason: if var(tau_j) = A + B/pop_j with A, B >= 0 (Ferman-Pinto's var(W_j|M_j) = A + B/M_j; the scaled SE alone imposes A = 0), then E[SE_s^2] = A mean_j(pop_j)/pop_u + B/pop_u and E[SE_n^2] = A + B mean_j(1/pop_j), against the truth A + B/pop_u. For California, larger than every donor, SE_s is at or below the truth and SE_n at or above it for every A, B >= 0, so the max is conservative for California itself, whatever the mix of state-level shocks (A) and size-related noise (B). It is not shown conservative if the variance rises with size (B < 0); the level check on large units is the check for that. Diagnostic, reported and never used for a decision: Ferman-Pinto's own step 3, OLS of tau_j^2 on 1 and 1/pop_j over the J placebos, giving A_hat, B_hat and SE_FP = sqrt(max(0, A_hat + B_hat/pop_u)). DEGREES OF FREEDOM (design-r3 D13; fixed now, whatever check-methods shows): every label uses t at nu = min(J, nu_hat), never t_J. For California every weight pop_j/pop_CA is below 1, so SE_s < SE_n in every run and California's SE is SE_n, the root mean of J squared placebo estimates whose variances s_j^2 differ across donors. Its Satterthwaite df is (sum_j s_j^2)^2 / sum_j s_j^4, which equals J only when the s_j^2 are equal (about 13 for D20 in the hetero-A Monte Carlo design). nu_hat is that formula with s_j^2 = mean over the six pseudo-dates of tau_j(B')^2, where tau_j(B') is donor j's placebo estimate of the same statistic in California's level-check test (level-mde, data ending 2019Q4), so nu is fixed for every statistic before any post-2023Q3 outcome is read. A run whose donor set is a subset of the pool (rob-7225) computes nu_hat over its own donors and caps it at its own J. With about two independent draws per donor the estimated s_j^2 are dispersed, which biases nu_hat downward (to roughly J/2 when the true variances are equal), so intervals are somewhat wider than at the true df. No correction is applied; the cost shows in MDE_h1, MDE_h2, MDE_h3, h90 and the label probabilities, which use the same nu. The penalty also applies where it is not needed (design-r4 D14): when donor variances differ because of size (B_hat > 0), E[SE_n^2] = A + B mean_j(1/pop_j) already exceeds California's A + B/pop_CA, so SE_n is conservative for California, yet the same size-driven differences make nu_hat small, and t at nu widens the interval a second time. This is accepted, not corrected: nu stays min(J, nu_hat) with no floor. So that the paper can show how much of the width is the df penalty, level-mde also reports MDE_h2 and h90 computed with t_J in place of t_nu (in the t floor of each critical value and in the power quantile; L quantiles unchanged) next to the t_nu values and next to nu_hat and nu; these t_J values are report-only and no label uses them. t quantiles and cdfs at non-integer df come from scipy.stats.t. Each run reports nu_hat and nu. Critical values c_hi(p), c_lo(p) come from LEVEL CHECK below; each is at least as far from 0 as the t_nu quantile. Two-sided 95% CI = [tau - c_hi(0.975) SE, tau - c_lo(0.025) SE]; 90% CI = [tau - c_hi(0.95) SE, tau - c_lo(0.05) SE]; the one-sided 5% test (H1) rejects if tau/SE > c_hi(0.95). P-values from t_nu are reported for information; every label uses the CIs. A 5% test is attainable without California ranking first among the placebos (with D20, J = 20; with R50, J = 50; rob-7225 lists its own J). LEVEL CHECK (run level-mde; truncated input state_panel_pre.csv only; after the design gate and before any run that reads a post-2023Q3 outcome; design-r1 D1-D3): statistics checked: for the selected candidate, pooled W (H1), pooled E-or-P (H2) and the year-2-minus-year-1 difference (H3); the pooled H2 statistic of S1 and of S2 at the same pseudo-dates (S1: AGG, E, R50, endpoint trend (g_B' - g_B'-8)/8; S2: SDID, P, D20, fit window 2015Q1..B'); and the pooled H2 statistic of the selected estimator and outcome with the other pool (for rob-pool). At each of the six pseudo-dates B', for each unit u in the pool plus California, INFERENCE is applied with u treated. California uses the pool (J donors). Every other unit u uses donors D_u = pool minus u (J-1 donors), with California excluded both from its donor set and from its placebos, so no placebo-unit test carries California's 2014-2019 minimum-wage ramp through the comparison (design-r2 D8); its t reference is t_{J-1}. T_u = tau_u/SE_u. For each statistic, and separately with SE, SE_s and SE_n, level-mde reports the empirical rates of T > t_{0.95}, T < -t_{0.95} and |T| > t_{0.975} (t at J for California, at J-1 for the other units; California's rates are also reported at t_nu): (i) over all 6(J+1) tests; (ii) by population tercile of the J+1 units at B'; (iii) over the decision set L; (iv) for California's six tests, with the diagnostic k = RMS of California's six T values. DECISION SET L (D1, D3): the ten most populous D20 states at each B' (60 tests). They are the large units among the states whose binding minimum was the federal $7.25 throughout 2014-2019 (verified by task s-mw-history), so their pseudo-ATTs have no own-policy content, unlike California's and many R50 states'; with California excluded from their donors and placebos, their D20-pool comparisons have no policy content either. For the R50-pool statistics (S1 and, if the primary uses D20, the other-pool statistic) an L unit's donors still include R50 states with their own 2014-2019 increases (T17 ii). L contains no unit as large as California, so it can detect over-rejection that grows with size but cannot measure California's own level; that is what the max SE is for. EFFECTIVE DRAWS (D2): the six post windows (2016Q4-2018Q3 to 2018Q1-2019Q4) overlap by 3 to 7 of 8 quarters, so one unit's six tests are about two independent draws: about 2(J+1) independent draws over all tests (42 for D20, 102 for R50) and about 20 in L. CRITICAL VALUES (D2; no threshold and no choice between variants): for each statistic, c_hi(p) = max(t_{nu,p}, empirical p-quantile of its 60 T values in L, numpy method 'higher'; the L values come from J-1 donors, which makes their tails, if anything, slightly wider than at J) for p in {0.95, 0.975}, and c_lo(p) = min(-t_{nu,1-p}, empirical p-quantile, method 'lower') for p in {0.025, 0.05}. For an SDID statistic (S2, and every statistic of an SDID candidate if select picks one) each critical value is also at least as far from 0 as the Monte Carlo floor of the pool the run uses: c_hi(p) = max(t_{nu,p}, L quantile, q_cal,hi(p)) and c_lo(p) = min(-t_{nu,1-p}, L quantile, q_cal,lo(p)) (CHECK-METHODS CONSEQUENCES C1). With 60 values the 0.025 and 0.975 quantiles are the second smallest and second largest: attainable, but noisy with about 20 independent draws; that noise can only widen an interval relative to t_nu, never narrow it. Use: the selected candidate's H1, H2 and H3 values apply to h1-wage, h2-emp, h3-years and the corresponding anticip statistics; S1's to sec-cemn; S2's to sec-dube; the other-pool value to rob-pool; the selected candidate's H2 value, with t at each run's own nu (its own J and nu_hat over its own donors), to the other robustness and placebo runs and to event-path bands. The rates are reported against 0.05 with a binomial band on the effective draws; they are evidence, not a switch. The design gate therefore approves a rule whose winner is unknown together with an inference procedure fixed for any winner; its empirical level is documented by level-mde before any post-2023Q3 outcome is read (F15b). MDE AND POWER (level-mde; design-r1 D6): SE_pre = sqrt(mean over B' of SE_CA(B')^2) for each statistic, with SE = max(SE_s, SE_n); SE_s,pre and SE_n,pre are reported too. MDE at 80% power: MDE_h2 = (c_hi(0.975) + t_{nu,0.80}) SE_pre, MDE_h3 likewise, MDE_h1 = (c_hi(0.95) + t_{nu,0.80}) SE_pre (one-sided). For H2's size label, an equivalence statement: h90 = max(c_hi(0.95), -c_lo(0.05)) SE_pre, the 90% CI half-width, reported against b = 0.02 ('no effect as large as 2%' is reachable only if h90 < b); and the probability of each of the nine H2 labels under tau = 0 and under tau = -0.035, computed from tau_hat = tau + SE_pre T with T ~ t_nu and the CI rule above (closed form from the t_nu cdf; no simulation). MDE_h2, h90 and the label probabilities are reported next to H2. If MDE_h3 > 0.04, H3 is reported as uninformative whatever its estimate. SE_pre rests on 2014-2019 noise and on seasonal factors fitted on the same years (T7, T13), so it is a lower bound: h2-emp and h3-years report MDE_h2, h90 and MDE_h3 recomputed with the real post-period SE next to the level-mde values (report-only; the H3 uninformative rule uses the larger of the two MDE_h3 values). DECISIONS (verdict run; exactly the approved rules): H1 supported if the pooled W statistic rejects the one-sided 5% test. If not, H2 is reported as uninformative about the wage floor. H2: sign from the 95% CI [L, U], size from the 90% CI [l, u] against b = 0.02, and the label from the nine-cell table in hypotheses[1]. H3: 95% CI of tau_2 - tau_1 below 0 means 'larger decline in year two', above 0 means 'smaller decline in year two', otherwise 'no detectable change'. Own-wage elasticities (pooled and yearly; design-r1 D5) = employment ATT / wage ATT, where the wage ATT in the denominator re-applies the selected candidate to log weekly wage with the employment fit reused (SC: the employment w; SDID: the employment omega and, per window, the employment lambda; DD and DDT have no fitted weights, so their H1 wage ATT is already this one, with the DDT trend fitted on wages). Numerator and denominator then use one comparison, which is what makes dilution by uncovered establishments roughly cancel, and it matches the reused-weights wage effect on which the -0.29 elasticity behind b was calibrated. For SC and SDID the ratio with the H1 (refitted) wage ATT is reported next to it, marked 'refitted wage weights'. An elasticity is computed only for windows whose H1 wage effect rejects the one-sided 5% test and whose reused-weights wage ATT is positive, otherwise 'not computed'. Point values only. MULTIPLE TESTING: no family-wise correction. H2 is the single primary employment test, H1 is a gate for reading it, and H3 is a separately labelled secondary with its own MDE rule. Secondaries, robustness checks and placebos are reported with CIs and rule labels marked 'not the headline'; they never create a new finding, but S1, S2 and runs 9, 10, 11 and 13 can qualify the headline (verdict; design-r1 D4). The paper says that with two placebo outcomes a chance 'failure' of one at 95% has probability of about 0.10. ORDER AFTER THE GATE: select, then level-mde, then any run that reads post-2023Q3 outcomes. Each post-period script declares runs/select/metrics.json and runs/level-mde/metrics.json as --input and takes the candidate and inference variant from them; nothing is hard-coded. select is run once. If a reviewed bug fix forces a rerun with --replace, the superseded record stays under runs/.superseded and the paper reports every selection run and its winner. CHECK-METHODS CONSEQUENCES (Designer, 2026-11-21, after the first check-methods run, which read only synthetic panels built on the 2016Q1 populations, the seasonal-factor rows and Prop 99; no study placebo, RMSE or outcome had been computed. Design review had used its four rounds, so each rule below says which existing rule it follows from; the code review checks the code against it and the human sees it at the design gate). C1 (from analysis_plan 0f: 'a failure of (a) is returned to the Designer before the design gate; it is not tuned away'). (iv)(a) failed in one cell: SDID-E, D20, pure A, rho = 0, with SE = max(SE_s, SE_n) at t_J: upper 0.067, lower 0.051, two-sided 0.0705 against 0.05 + band = 0.0646. Every DD, DDT and SC cell passed. The floor applies with both pools although only the D20 cell failed, because the cause is in the estimator and the R50 cells (R = 500) are too few to rule it out. For SDID this replaces (a) at t_J; the t_J rates stay reported next to it as the uncorrected rates (the D20 rho = 0 cell fails there again, as recorded above). A failure of (a-SDID) is a bug to look for, as for a Prop 99 miss, and rv-code checks any fix; if none is found the floor is not re-tuned and the design does not come back: the measured rates stand in T6 and the paper, every SDID label (S2, or the primary if SDID is selected) is marked 'size above 5% in check-methods', and the design gate is requested with that on record. Limit: the floor comes from the pseudo-date geometry of (iv) (fit window 2014Q1-2017Q2, eight-quarter post window), not from S2's real fit window (2015Q1-2023Q3 without C), so it transfers to the real runs by assumption; it can only widen an SDID interval. The selection rule, its 24 candidates and their order are unchanged, and S2's label enters the verdict as before. C2 (from analysis_plan 0f: 'if no bug is found, the measured rates stand'). (iv)(b) failed in one cell, SDID-E, D20, hetero-A, rho = 0 (nu_MC 13.19): two-sided 0.0765 at t_J against r2 + band = 0.0725, and 0.0700 at t_{nu_MC} against 0.0646; the one-sided rates are within their bounds (t_J 0.0565 and 0.065; t_{nu_MC} 0.054 and 0.0595), and every other hetero-A cell passed. No bug was found, so nothing changes: T6 and the paper cite 0.070 (two-sided, at t_{nu_MC}) as California's size under hetero-A for SDID with D20, next to the same cell's hetero-A-CA2 rate (0.170 at t_{nu_MC}, 0.1825 at t_J, nu_MC 13.32). It applies to S2 and to an SDID primary. The check-methods rerun judges (b) as before; it is expected to fail again in this cell with the same draws, which is this recorded result, not a new failure. The rerun also reports SDID's hetero-A and hetero-A-CA2 rates with the C1 floor (report-only; they decide nothing). C3 (from analysis_plan 0f (i): the check tests the code, and 'a miss is a bug to find, not a reason to change the algorithm'). The first run gave SC -19.514, outside the printed -19.6's interval [-19.65, -19.55). The exact minimiser of the stated objective (no intercept, zeta = 1e-6 sigma_hat, no time weights) is -19.514 both by sclib's SLSQP (KKT 1.6e-8) and by an independent solve; a diagnostic port of synthdid's Frank-Wolfe solver gives -19.587 without and -19.620 with its default sparsification. The printed value is therefore a property of synthdid's solver (its stopping rule and its sparsification), which this design does not use: design.method SOFTWARE fixes exact minimisation checked by KKT to 1e-6. The SC part of (i) is replaced by two conditions. (i-SC-1) the objective is minimised: sclib's estimate equals, to within 1e-3 packs, that of an exact solve in test_sclib.py that shares no code with sclib's simplex_ls (an active-set or NNLS solve, its own KKT residual <= 1e-6), and sclib's KKT residual is <= 1e-6. A failure means sclib's weight solver does not minimise the design's objective; the same solver fits every SC and SDID weight, so it is a bug to find before the code review. (i-SC-2) the objective is the paper's: the Frank-Wolfe port of synthdid (pinned commit 70c1ce3; its defaults: 100 iterations, then weights at or below max/4 set to 0 and renormalised, then up to 10,000 iterations; min_decrease 1e-5 sigma_hat), fed the objective's inputs (the Prop 99 matrix, sigma_hat and the penalty) from the same sclib functions the study uses, lies in [-19.65, -19.55). A failure means the data, sigma_hat, the penalty or the no-intercept form differ from what Arkhangelsky et al. computed: a bug to find in those inputs, not a reason to change the solver. The unsparsified port value is reported next to it. DID and SDID keep their printed-value conditions, which the exact solver meets. The paper reports the SC triple (exact, Frank-Wolfe unsparsified, Frank-Wolfe sparsified) and says that our SC and SDID weights are exact minimisers, which on Prop 99 differ from synthdid's output by about 0.1 packs for SC. C4 (new rule; the old name breaks Python imports): code/select.py is renamed code/select_rule.py wherever the design names it. The run id stays 'select' (runs/select/...). IMPLEMENTATION CHOICES (runs/NOTES.md items 1-14; each is adopted into this design as stated there unless marked changed). 1 changed: select.py is renamed select_rule.py (C4); test_sclib.py imports it under its own name. 2 adopted: SLSQP solves the objective divided by b'b (same minimiser; scale-free ftol and KKT residual); while the KKT residual exceeds 1e-7 it is restarted from its own solution with the same options, at most 3 times, and a restart is kept only if the residual falls; the reported residual is that of the normalised problem; unpenalised intercepts (omega0, lambda0) are profiled out exactly by centring. 0f. check-methods (data-prep, econometrician, code/test_sclib.py importing code/sclib.py; synthetic data and Prop 99 only; task e-check; before the code review). (i) Prop 99 (39 states, 1970-2000, treated from 1989; T_pre = 19, T_post = 12, N_co = 38, N_tr = 1; zeta = (1 * 12)^(1/4) sigma_hat): the DID and SDID estimates must round to the value Arkhangelsky et al. (2021) Table 1 prints to one decimal (claim c-sdid-prop99; notes section 9 item 9), i.e. lie in the printed value's rounding interval: DID -27.3, [-27.35, -27.25); SDID -15.6, [-15.65, -15.55); SC without intercept (zeta = 1e-6 sigma_hat, no time weights; the paper's SC, printed -19.6): the two conditions of design.method C3 instead of the printed value (i-SC-1: sclib's estimate equals an independent exact solve to within 1e-3, KKT <= 1e-6; i-SC-2: the Frank-Wolfe port of synthdid with its default sparsification, fed sclib's objective inputs, lies in [-19.65, -19.55)). The script also prints each estimate to three decimals. sigma_hat and both penalties as design.method SDID (eq. 2.2; unit penalty zeta^2 T_pre ||omega||^2; time penalty (1e-6 sigma_hat)^2 N_co ||lambda||^2, fn 3). A miss is a bug to find, not a reason to change the algorithm. (ii) Synthetic panels with one treated unit, 20 and 50 donors and a known effect: DD/DDT closed forms equal an OLS TWFE with unit and time effects (plus unit trends for DDT), population weights included, to 1e-10; SC and SDID recover exact weights when the treated unit is a convex combination; demeaned SC equals the SDID routine with zeta = 0 and uniform time weights; the KKT conditions hold to 1e-6. (iii) Seasonal factors computed from state_panel_pre.csv equal those computed from state_panel.csv. (iv) Monte Carlo of the inference (design-r1 D1): synthetic panels with the real 2016Q1 populations of California plus D20 and of California plus R50 (population only, from state_panel_pre.csv; no outcome column read), 2014Q1-2019Q4, unit and quarter effects, California treated at B' = 2017Q2, true effect 0, errors e_jt = a_jt + u_jt with Gaussian a_jt of variance sigma_A^2 (state-level shock) and u_jt of variance sigma_B^2 pop_med/pop_j (size-related noise), each AR(1) with rho in {0, 0.5}, in five designs: pure B (sigma_A = 0), pure A (sigma_B = 0), mixed (sigma_A = sigma_B, equal at the median state), and two pure-A designs with heterogeneous state-shock variances (design-r2 D12): hetero-A, in which the five oil states ND, WY, OK, LA and TX have sigma_A,j^2 = 4 sigma_A^2, every other donor sigma_A^2, and California the mean of its donors' sigma_A,j^2 (so E[SE_n^2] is right and only the reduced effective degrees of freedom act: Satterthwaite df about 13 for D20 against J = 20); and hetero-A-CA2, the same with California at twice that mean (the T6 risk of California-specific noise); ten designs in all. Estimators: DD-POPW-E and DDT-POPW-E with both pools and SC-E and SDID-E with D20, 2,000 replications each; SC-E and SDID-E with R50, 500 replications. Plus the SDID calibration draws of design.method C1 (pure A, rho 0 and 0.5; D20 4,000 and R50 1,000 replications each; default_rng(20261122)), which give q_cal,hi(0.95), q_cal,hi(0.975), q_cal,lo(0.05) and q_cal,lo(0.025) per pool, written to metrics.json. For every design, estimator, pool and rho the script reports nu_MC = min(J, (sum_j s_j^2)^2 / sum_j s_j^4), with s_j^2 the variance of donor j's placebo estimate across the R replications (the design's own Satterthwaite df for SE_n, which is California's SE; design.method DEGREES OF FREEDOM), and California's rejection rates at t_J and at t_{nu_MC}. Testing at t_J or t_{nu_MC} without the L quantile is stricter than the real procedure, whose c is at least as far from 0 and whose estimated nu is biased downward. Pass conditions, stated in the script before it runs (R = replications; band(r) = 3*sqrt(r(1-r)/R)): (a) pure B, pure A and mixed: with SE = max(SE_s, SE_n) and t_J critical values, California's one-sided 5% tests (upper and lower tails) and two-sided 5% test each reject at most 0.05 + band(0.05). For SDID-E this is judged as (a-SDID) of design.method C1: the same bound with critical values max(t_J, q_cal,hi) and min(-t_J, q_cal,lo) on these replications; its t_J rates are reported as uncorrected. (b) hetero-A (design-r3 D13): it is judged against the rate the t_J test has when the statistic is t at nu_MC, not against 0.05: r1 = 1 - F_{nu_MC}(t_{J,0.95}) for each one-sided tail and r2 = 2(1 - F_{nu_MC}(t_{J,0.975})) two-sided (0.054 and 0.057 at nu_MC = 13, J = 20). Each t_J rate must be at most r + band(r), and each rate at t_{nu_MC} at most 0.05 + band(0.05). (c) hetero-A-CA2 is report-only: it measures how far California's rate exceeds 0.05 when California is noisier than its donors, the failure the max SE is not built to absorb. Its rates are reported at t_J and at t_{nu_MC}, with its own nu_MC (design-r4 D15); the rate at t_{nu_MC} is the one T6 and the paper cite as California's size under that design, because every label uses t at nu, and the t_J rate is shown next to it. Reported in every outcome: for each estimator, pool and rho, the hetero-A rates at t_J and at t_{nu_MC} and nu_MC, next to the pure-A rates (the excess caused by the df effect) and the hetero-A-CA2 rates at t_J and at t_{nu_MC} with its nu_MC; the scaled-only rates next to them (expected to exceed 0.05 under pure A and mixed). What follows, fixed now: no outcome of (b) or (c) changes the estimator, the SE, nu or the critical-value rule, and neither returns the design to the Designer; every label uses t at nu whatever (iv) shows. If (b) passes, the paper says the hetero-A excess at t_J is the df effect the plan predicts and that t at nu removes it. If (b) fails, it is treated as a bug to find in sclib.py or test_sclib.py, as for a Prop 99 miss: the Econometrician looks for it, rv-code checks any fix, and the rates before and after the fix are both reported. T4 AB 257 (enacted September 2022, a possible $22 fast-food wage, stayed January 2023, replaced by AB 1228; literature-r1 L1): 2022Q3-2023Q3, including the 2023Q3 base and the end of every real fit window, falls under a pending sectoral wage law. T6 Inference with one treated state (design-r1 D1): the population-scaled placebo SE alone assumes var(tau_j) proportional to 1/pop_j (Ferman-Pinto A = 0). State QCEW 722513 is a near-census, so state-level shocks (A > 0) are likely, and then the scaled SE understates California's SE because California is larger than every donor, while a level check pooled over all units can pass because small units under-reject. Handled by: SE = max(scaled, unscaled), conservative for the largest unit for any A, B >= 0; critical values never below t at nu = min(J, estimated Satterthwaite df of SE_n) and widened by the over-rejection of the ten most populous policy-free D20 states (not by a pooled rate); rates reported by population tercile, for L and for California; the Ferman-Pinto A_hat, B_hat diagnostic; and a check-methods Monte Carlo with A > 0 designs, including heterogeneous state-shock variances (oil states at four times the variance), where t_J would be optimistic because SE_n has fewer effective degrees of freedom than J (design-r2 D12); the labels therefore use t at nu whatever the Monte Carlo shows, and hetero-A is judged against the rate expected at its own df, with its excess at t_J reported next to the pure-A rate (design-r3 D13). Remaining risk: variance rising with size (B < 0) or California-specific noise beyond size; L contains no unit as large as California, so its level for California is argued, not measured. The hetero-A-CA2 Monte Carlo design shows the size of the over-rejection if California's state-shock variance is twice its donors' mean; it cannot say whether it is. The figure cited here and in the paper is its rate at t_{nu_MC}, the critical value the labels use, with the t_J rate next to it (design-r4 D15). Cost: wider intervals, shown by MDE_h2, h90 and the label probabilities. The df penalty also applies where SE_n is already conservative for California (donor variances differing because of size, B_hat > 0), so there the interval is widened twice; this is accepted (nu = min(J, nu_hat), no floor), and level-mde reports MDE_h2 and h90 under t_J next to the t_nu values so the paper can show how much of the width is the df penalty (design-r4 D14). First check-methods run (design.method C1, C2): SDID's placebo t has heavier tails than t_J even under pure A (two-sided 0.0705 at t_J, D20, rho = 0; no bug found), so every SDID statistic uses a Monte Carlo floor on its critical values, validated on replications independent of the calibration draws; the floor comes from the pseudo-date geometry and transfers to S2's real windows by assumption. Under hetero-A, SDID-E with D20 at rho = 0 rejects two-sided at 0.070 at t_{nu_MC} (nu_MC 13.19; one-sided 0.054 and 0.0595), above 0.05 + band = 0.0646, with no bug found: that is California's measured size for this combination under hetero-A, cited next to the same cell's hetero-A-CA2 rate (0.170 at t_{nu_MC}, 0.1825 at t_J). It applies to S2 and to an SDID primary; every other hetero-A cell passed.

T7 MDE from 2014-2019 noise may understate post-COVID noise: the real SE from h2-emp is reported next to MDE_h2, and MDE_h2, h90 and MDE_h3 are recomputed with it (the H3 rule uses the larger MDE_h3).

T8 Donor contamination: R50 states that raised their minimum wages during 2024-2026 bias the R50 estimate toward a smaller decline. D20 states have no minimum-wage change but differ economically. rob-pool and S1 versus S2 show the difference.

T9 Treated sector is wider than and different from 722513: covered chains sit in 722515 (never used) and in 722511 (Melo et al. 7.9% of chain locations in Louisiana; L2). 722511 is therefore reported as a non-clean placebo only (plc-722511) and is never a DDD control. Classification can change with the policy: rob-7225.

T10 Dilution: tau is an intent-to-treat effect on all of 722513. Melo et al. put California covered-chain employment (YTS) about one third below QCEW 722513 in 2025, an approximation from another universe; no rescaling is done. The own-wage elasticity is roughly invariant to dilution. Measurement across states and over time (literature-r2 L11): Melo et al. argue that QCEW 722513 may track covered-chain employment poorly both at a point in time and as a trend, and across donor states (2019-2025 QCEW-minus-YTS changes of -8 to +17 points, far wider than the 2% bound), which can distort the counterfactual; the YTS benchmark is itself modelled data, so this is a contested objection, not a known bias. The design cannot remove it: the placebo SE samples only donor divergence present in 2014-2019, and rob-pool and S1 versus S2 show sensitivity to donor composition but not to measurement. The paper reports it as a limit: the estimand is defined on QCEW 722513, the H2 equivalence verdict is a statement about QCEW 722513, and the paper does not claim tau equals the effect on covered establishments.

T11 QCEW counts jobs held in the pay period including the 12th, not hours; weekly earnings are not the hourly wage, so H1 is biased toward zero if hours fell, and lower turnover can lower counts (Dube App. B). Stated as limits; no fix.

T12 Concurrent California shocks: the general minimum wage rises (affecting uncovered 722513 and 722511 workers), SB 525 (health care, from October 2024), and California's slower population growth (per-capita candidates; Census extrapolation for 2025Q3-2026Q1 matters only if a P candidate wins). plc-nonff is the check; a failure qualifies H2.

T13 Seasonal factors are estimated on 2014-2019, the years of the pseudo-windows, which flatters every candidate's placebo RMSE about equally and flatters SE_pre and hence the MDE and h90 (design-r1 D6; the post-period recomputation in T7 is the check). Stale factors after COVID mostly average out over two full post years, except at the single Q3 base: event-path, rob-base-2023q4 (a Q4 base).
T14 Data revisions: 2026Q1 is preliminary and 2025 will be revised. The vintage is pinned by the manifest hashes; rob-final-quarters drops 2026Q1.
T15 Nominal wages: differential price changes between California and donors enter H1. Stated.

T16 Code errors: check-methods (Prop 99 against Arkhangelsky et al. Table 1, synthetic identities, Monte Carlo level), code review before any analysis run, the published cross-checks in sec-cemn and sec-dube, and a clean rerun. The Prop 99 SC check tests the design's objective, not synthdid's solver (design.method C3): our exact minimum is -19.514 against the printed -19.6, which synthdid's Frank-Wolfe solver with sparsification gives. Demeaned SC weights are not unique when the fit window is shorter than the donor count, so SC estimates are those of the fixed deterministic solver; select reports the gap to an independent solve (IMPLEMENTATION CHOICES 3).

T17 The pre-period is not policy-free (design-r1 D3): California's general minimum wage rose every year from July 2014 to $15 in 2022 (Wiltshire et al.), the D20 donors stayed at $7.25, and many R50 states raised theirs in 2014-2019. (i) Selection: California's pseudo-ATTs contain the relative effect of that ramp, so the rule rewards candidates that track it (a gap trend, DDT, or donors with their own increases, R50), whether or not they reproduce the AB 1228-free path after 2023, when the general minimum rose more slowly. The premise is restated accordingly (identifying_assumption), and the paper says that an R50 or DDT winner may reflect the shared ramp. (ii) Level check: R50 units treated at pseudo-dates carry their own increases, so their T values are not null draws; the critical values therefore use only L, the ten most populous D20 states (federal minimum throughout 2014-2019, s-mw-history), and rates over all units are reported as context. (iii) MDE: SE_pre uses donor placebos and is reported as a lower bound (T7). S1 and S2 can qualify the headline (verdict).
